messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 69
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Nanny
  trauma_type: Child's life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 71

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Medical Care: Seeking medical or psychological help, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time
  Memory: No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself, More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things, Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
  Negative Appraisals: Unrecognisable Self: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me, Distrust Others: People are not what they seem, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Boun sits stiffly on the edge of the armchair, his hands clasped so tightly the knuckles are white. At sixty-nine, he is a man accustomed to perpetual motion, and the stillness of the therapy office feels unnatural, almost threatening. It was his employer, a kind young woman whose children he cares for, who finally insisted he come. For months, a dry, rattling cough has settled deep in his chest, a cough he refuses to take to a doctor. The very idea of a clinic waiting room, the smell of antiseptic, the detached authority of a physician—it is a door he cannot bring himself to open.

It all goes back to the winter his daughter, Dara, was seven. The memory isn’t a story he can tell, not even to himself. It exists in him as a series of blindingly clear, disconnected fragments. There is the memory of Dara’s forehead, impossibly hot under his palm. There is the memory of the fluorescent lights of the emergency room humming over his head, a sound that felt like a physical weight. He can recall, with a clarity that eclipses the memory of his own wedding day, the exact shade of blue on the blanket they wrapped her in, and the rhythmic, terrifying beep of the heart monitor that became the soundtrack to his life for weeks. When he tries to piece the days together, to form a coherent narrative of what happened, his mind goes blank. There are gaps, whole days missing, replaced only by the phantom sensation of the cold vinyl of a waiting room chair on the backs of his legs. When a memory does break through, it feels less like a recollection and more like a sudden, violent teleportation. The memory is not in the past; it is happening right now. He is back in that sterile room, watching his daughter’s small chest struggle for air, the feeling of absolute helplessness washing over him as if for the first time.

In the years that followed Dara’s eventual, miraculous recovery, Boun learned to outrun his own mind. He and his late wife never spoke of that time. It was an unspoken agreement to build a wall of silence around the experience. After she passed, the silence became a cavern, and he took the job as a nanny to fill it with the noise of children’s laughter and demands. His days are now a masterclass in mental distraction. He throws himself into his work with a ferocious energy that his employers mistake for simple dedication. He builds elaborate Lego castles, reads picture books with exaggerated voices, and organizes the playroom with meticulous precision, all in a desperate effort to keep his mind occupied. Any moment of quiet is a danger zone. “Don’t think about it,” he tells himself a hundred times a day, scrubbing a dish or folding a tiny t-shirt. “Just focus on this.” The effort leaves him utterly exhausted by evening.

This constant vigilance has changed him. He looks in the mirror and sees a stranger. The man he used to be—calm, patient, trusting—is gone. He has come to believe that the experience permanently damaged something essential inside him. He sees this new, broken self most clearly at work. When four-year-old Leo scraped his knee at the park last week, Boun’s reaction was so swift and panicked that it frightened the boy more than the fall itself. He feels a deep, gnawing distrust of the world now. The doctors at the hospital had offered shifting diagnoses and reassurances that felt hollow; he came to see them not as helpers, but as gatekeepers of a truth they were unwilling to share. This suspicion has since bled into everything. He is certain that people are not what they seem, that his employers are secretly judging his every move, that the other nannies at the playground are whispering about him.

He is here now because that distrust has finally turned inward, paralyzing him. His own body is sending warning signs, but he cannot bring himself to seek medical care. To him, a doctor’s office is not a place of healing, but a place where your life is taken out of your hands, where you are made small and powerless. He has chosen the familiar pain of his memories over the terrifying unknown of a diagnosis. But his employer’s ultimatum has left him with no choice. He doesn’t believe he can ever go back to the man he was before the hospital, but he is terrified of losing his job, of being left alone in the quiet with nothing but the beeping of the machine in his memory.
